title: Osso Buco
subtitle: Braised beef shin with a bright gremolata finish
excerpt: This is a long, slow braise from Milan, traditionally made with veal but equally good with beef shin. The gremolata of lemon, parsley, and garlic cuts through the richness at the end.
sourceNotes: Osso buco alla milanese is a Lombardy classic dating to the 19th century. Beef shin is used here as a direct substitute for veal shank, sharing the same gelatinous quality.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the braised shin (without gremolata) for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if needed.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily in a large stockpot. Brown the shin in batches so the pan stays hot.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The braise improves the next day. Make it a day ahead and reheat gently.

content.text: Proper browning is the foundation of this dish. Take the time to get good colour on the beef before adding any liquid, or the braise will taste flat.

items.prepNote: 4 cloves roughly crushed for the braise, 2 cloves finely minced for gremolata

content.text: Pat the beef shin dry with kitchen paper. Season all over with salt and pepper.
Heat a splash of oil in the stockpot over high heat. Brown the shin pieces in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deeply coloured. Set aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 8 minutes, stirring often, until softened. Add the 4 crushed garlic cloves and cook for 1 minute more.
Pour in the white wine vinegar and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits from the base of the pot.
Add the tinned tomatoes, chicken stock, thyme, and bay leaves. Return the beef to the pot. The liquid should come about halfway up the shin. Bring to a simmer.
Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 2 hours, turning the shin once halfway through, until the meat is very tender and falling from the bone.
Make the gremolata: combine the finely minced garlic, chopped parsley, and lemon zest in a small bowl.
Serve the shin on its braising vegetables with a spoonful of gremolata scattered over the top.

items.symptom: The meat is tough after 2 hours.
items.cause: The braise was too vigorous or the cut was very thick.
items.fix: Continue cooking; check every 20 minutes until tender.

items.symptom: The sauce is very thin and watery.
items.cause: The lid was off or the heat too high, reducing the liquid.
items.fix: Remove the meat, boil the sauce for 10 minutes to concentrate it.

items.symptom: The meat has fallen apart completely.
items.cause: It was cooked a little too long.
items.fix: Serve as-is; it will still taste excellent in the braising juices.
